beats.text: In January twenty twenty-one, some of the most powerful investors on Wall Street bet that a struggling video game shop would collapse.
A man on the internet in a red headband had bet about fifty-three thousand dollars that they were wrong.
Within weeks, his position was worth nearly forty-eight million dollars. And one of the funds betting against him needed billions to keep going.
This is the GameStop story, explained like you're five.
GameStop sold video games in shopping malls. But people had started downloading games instead of buying discs.
Then the pandemic shut the malls. So a lot of big investors looked at GameStop and saw a business that was dying.
When big investors think a company will fail, they can bet on it. It's called short selling.
Imagine you borrow your friend's toy car. It's worth ten dollars. You sell it straight away, for ten dollars.
Next week, toy cars drop to two dollars. You buy one back for two, give it to your friend, and keep eight dollars.
That's a short. You win when the price falls.
But here's the catch. What if the price goes up instead? You still owe your friend a toy car. You have to buy one back, whatever it costs.
When you buy something, the most you can lose is what you paid. When you short something, there's no limit.
With GameStop, so many funds were shorting that something strange happened.
More shares had been sold short than were actually available to trade. America's market regulator later put short interest at nearly a hundred and twenty-three percent of the shares available.
It's like borrowing and selling more toy cars than there are in the whole playground.
One person had looked at the same company and seen something different.
Keith Gill, known online as Roaring Kitty, believed GameStop was worth far more than its price.
In twenty nineteen, he posted his position online. About fifty-three thousand dollars. And he kept posting updates, month after month, and making videos explaining why.
And people started to notice the trap the short sellers had built for themselves.
If the price started rising, the short sellers would have to buy shares back to stop their losses. And buying pushes the price up even more.
Which forces more short sellers to buy. Which pushes the price higher still. That's a short squeeze.
In January twenty twenty-one, huge numbers of ordinary people, many from an online forum called WallStreetBets, piled in.
On January eleventh, a GameStop share closed at about twenty dollars. By January twenty-seventh, it closed at three hundred and forty-seven.
The next morning, it touched four hundred and eighty-three dollars.
One of the funds caught on the wrong side was called Melvin Capital.
Melvin lost more than half its money in January. It took two point seven five billion dollars from two other firms, Citadel and Point72, to keep going.
Short sellers as a group lost billions of dollars in a matter of days.
Then, on January twenty-eighth, something happened that made people furious.
Robinhood, the trading app many of the new investors used, stopped customers from buying GameStop. Other brokers did the same. You could sell. You just couldn't buy.
The price dropped. People accused the brokers of protecting Wall Street.
The brokers said it was about the plumbing. To trade, they have to put up cash with a clearing house, and the wild swings meant they suddenly had to put up far more.
Congress held hearings. Regulators wrote a long report. But in those wild days, the buy button was gone.
So who won?
At its peak, Keith Gill's position was worth nearly forty-eight million dollars, on paper.
Some people who bought early made fortunes. Many who bought near the top, at three or four hundred dollars, lost a lot when the price fell back.
Melvin Capital closed down in twenty twenty-two.
The lesson isn't that the little guy always wins. Most of the time, he doesn't.
It's this. When you short a stock, you can lose more than everything you put in. And when too many people make the same bet, the exit gets very small.
Some of Wall Street's biggest players bet a dying video game shop would go to zero. The bet nearly sent one of them there instead.
